newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia says not involved in Timor meet incident.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia says not involved in Timor meet incident.

text.p: The Malaysian government said on Sunday it was not involved in the action of a youth group that broke up a controversial activists' conference on East Timor.

Deputy Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim was quoted by the national Bernama news agency as saying the government did not sanction Saturday's action although the youths involved belonged to groups allied to the three main political parties in Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad's coalition.
"They acted on their own. I was not notified by them. Well, certainly there was no sanction from the National Front (coalition)," he told reporters.

The group, calling itself the Malaysian Action Front, stormed into the second Asia Pacific Conference on East Timor being held in a hotel in central Kuala Lumpur, shouting slogans and singing patriotic songs.
Police later took 46 foreign activists away. Fifty-nine Malaysian human rights activists, two foreign journalists and seven members of the youth group that disrupted the meeting were also detained.
Immigration officials began deporting some of the foreigners on Sunday morning but as of midafternoon on Sunday the journalists were still being held.
A spokesman for the organisers has accused the government of orchestrating the incident to scuttle the conference.
But Anwar said, "That is their assumption. I cannot confirm it. They (the Malaysian Action Front members) acted on their own just as the NGOs (non-governmental organisations) acted on their own."
He said the police acted to calm the situation according to the law without regards to whether the people involved were NGO members or members of the Malaysian Action Front.

On whether wide foreign media coverage of the incident would damage the image of the government and country, Anwar said the holding of the conference itself was an attempt to embarrass the government and complicate Malaysia-Indonesia relations.
"Public order and our good relations with Indonesia are more important. The issue of East Timor should be pursued in a better way, through the usual channels," he said.
A Malaysian minister said earlier this week that the government did not want the conference to take place because it could harm bilateral ties with Indonesia.
Indonesia invaded East Timor in 1975 and now rules the territory in defiance of the United Nations.

A media spotlight is expected to be cast on Indonesia this week. Tuesday marks the anniversary of a bloody 1991 confrontation in the East Timor capital of Dili in which troops killed at least 50 demonstrators.
Witnesses and human rights groups have estimated around 200 people died.
